young.html: Francis Bacon lived in England about 400 years ago, in the time of Shakespeare. He was a lawyer and a judge, but his favorite question was a big one: what do people know, and what don't they know yet?

In 1605 he wrote a book for King James I called The Advancement of Learning. In the first half he says learning is worth the hard work. In the second half he makes a map of everything people know, like a map of a country, and he marks the places nobody has explored yet.

His map has three big parts, one for each power of the mind. Memory gives us history: what happened. Imagination gives us poetry and stories. Reason gives us philosophy and science: why things happen.

young.name: gb-bacon-map
young.cap: Tap a branch of Bacon's map to see what grows on it.

young.html: Bacon had a wise saying about doubt. If you start out sure of everything, you may end up confused. But if you start with honest questions, you can end up knowing something for sure.

Make your own map of learning. On a big sheet of paper, draw three branches: Memory, Imagination and Reason. Under each, write things you have learned: a story from history, a poem or book you love, a science fact. Then add a branch with a question mark for something you would like to find out.

full.html: Francis Bacon (1561–1626) was a lawyer, a member of Parliament and later Lord Chancellor of England. The Advancement of Learning (1605), written in English and dedicated to King James I, was his first large book about knowledge. He later expanded it in Latin as De Augmentis Scientiarum (1623). It is the survey that comes before his Novum Organum, the new method that has its own rung on this ladder.

full.text: Book One: why learning is worth it

full.html: Bacon first answers people who distrusted learning. Some churchmen said too much knowledge makes people proud; some statesmen said scholars make poor men of action; and some pointed to scholars' own faults. Bacon answers each in turn. He grants that learning has its diseases, which he calls distempers: “fantastical” learning (taking vain imaginations for truth), “contentious” learning (endless arguing about words) and “delicate” learning (caring more for fine style than for matter).

full.text: So it is in contemplation: if a man will begin with certainties, he shall end in doubts; but if he will be content to begin with doubts, he shall end in certainties.
full.author: Francis Bacon
full.work: The Advancement of Learning, First Book, V.8
full.ed: ed. Henry Morley, Cassell's National Library, Cassell & Company

full.html: The greatest error of all, Bacon says, is to mistake what learning is for. People study for curiosity, for delight, for reputation, to win arguments or to earn a living. Bacon lists these wrong ends in a run of images:

full.text: …as if there were sought in knowledge a couch whereupon to rest a searching and restless spirit; or a terrace for a wandering and variable mind to walk up and down with a fair prospect; or a tower of state, for a proud mind to raise itself upon; or a fort or commanding ground, for strife and contention; or a shop, for profit or sale; and not a rich storehouse for the glory of the Creator and the relief of man's estate.
full.author: Francis Bacon
full.work: The Advancement of Learning, First Book, V.11
full.ed: ed. Henry Morley, Cassell's National Library, Cassell & Company

full.html: “The relief of man's estate.” For Bacon, knowledge should serve two ends together: to honor God, as he saw it, and to make human life better. This hope, that learning should lead to useful works, runs through all his books.

full.text: Book Two: the map of learning

full.html: In the second book Bacon divides all human learning by the three powers of the mind: history belongs to memory, poesy (poetry and invented stories) to imagination, and philosophy to reason. Then he divides each again. History is natural, civil, church history and the history of learning itself. Poesy is narrative, dramatic, or allegorical (stories that carry a hidden meaning, like fables). Philosophy is about God as known by reason, about nature, and about human beings.

full.name: gb-bacon-map
full.cap: Bacon's division of learning. Open each branch; the gold notes are some of the gaps Bacon said were still “deficient.”

full.html: The most original part is his list of what is missing. Over and over Bacon writes that some field is “deficient”: there is no good history of the arts and trades, no history of learning itself, no true method for discovering new things rather than arguing about old ones. He is writing a to-do list for the next generations of scholars.
Thinking Bacon was against old books. He praises the ancients often and quotes them constantly. What he objects to is treating them as the end of learning instead of a beginning.

Bacon's call for a cooperative, useful science inspired the founders of the Royal Society of London (1660). When Diderot and d'Alembert planned the French Encyclopédie a century later, they arranged their “tree of knowledge” on Bacon's division into memory, imagination and reason, and said so. Critics then and now have pointed out that Bacon himself made few discoveries and undervalued mathematics, which Galileo, Kepler and Newton showed to be the language of the new physics.

deep.html: Bacon held that there are two books, Scripture and nature, and that both lead toward God. He drew a firm line between what reason can learn about the world and what faith receives by revelation, and he asked that the two not be mixed. Readers have argued ever since about whether this line protects religion, protects science, or both. Compare Pascal and Descartes later in this era.

Bacon is often summed up in the phrase “knowledge is power.” The idea is his (it appears in his Latin writings in several forms), and in the Advancement he pictures knowledge as a means of “works” that help people. Later writers asked hard questions about this hope: power for whom, and to do what? The question comes back in this ladder with Rousseau, Mill and others.

items: Is it better to start with doubts or with certainties? When might Bacon's advice go wrong?
Should learning always be useful? What about learning something just because it is beautiful?
Bacon listed fields that were “deficient” in 1605. What would you put on such a list today?

questions: Bacon says some people use learning like a “tower” to look down on others. Have you ever seen someone do that? How can we avoid it?
Which of Bacon's three powers, memory, imagination or reason, do you use most? Which is hardest for you?
What is something you started out sure about and later had doubts about?
If you could add one new branch to Bacon's map of learning, what would it be?
Is it fair to judge a book of science by how useful it turned out to be?
